exam.subject: Biology
exam.title: Eritrean Secondary Education Certificate Examinations 2020 – Biology (0056)

parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 60 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1.30 points. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Completion and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains thirteen completion and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty two points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Biology textbooks Grades 9–12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: The most related organisms are grouped in
explanation_steps: The taxonomic ranks run kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species.
The lower the rank, the fewer the organisms and the more features they share (the more closely related they are).
Of the ranks offered, family is the lowest, so it groups the most closely related organisms. Answer: A.
tips: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' – relationship increases towards Species.

similar_questions.stem: Which rank contains the greatest variety of organisms?
explanation_steps: Kingdom is the highest (broadest) rank. Answer: E.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 The importance of classification – levels of classification

questions.stem: A characteristic of life that deals with the sum total of all chemical reactions within an organism is
explanation_steps: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions that take place in a living organism – building up (anabolism, e.g. photosynthesis) and breaking down (catabolism, e.g. respiration).
Homeostasis = constant internal environment; responsiveness = reacting to stimuli. Answer: D.
tips: Metabolism = anabolism + catabolism.

similar_questions.stem: The breakdown of glucose to release energy in cells is an example of
explanation_steps: Breaking down large molecules = catabolism (part of metabolism). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 What is biology? – characteristics of living things

questions.stem: The scientific name of human beings is Homo sapiens. The name "Homo" represents
explanation_steps: In binomial nomenclature the first name (capitalised) is the genus and the second (lower case) is the specific epithet (species).
'Homo' is the genus – which is not among options A–D. Answer: E.
tips: Genus first, species second: Homo sapiens, Equus caballus, Zea mays.

similar_questions.stem: In the scientific name Felis catus (the domestic cat), 'catus' is the
explanation_steps: The second word is the species (specific epithet). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Viruses are not considered as living things because they
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.41): viruses have no nucleus, cytoplasm or cell membrane; they are not capable of metabolism and cannot replicate themselves unless they are inside host cells – 'therefore, outside host cells viruses are considered to be non-living particles'.
Having a capsid or nucleic acid does not make them non-living. The decisive reason given is that they cannot reproduce (or metabolise) on their own. Answer: E.
A (not made of cells) is also a valid reason given in the same paragraph.
tips: Viruses = obligate intracellular parasites: inert outside a host.

similar_questions.stem: Which feature of viruses is shared with living organisms?

options.C: They contain nucleic acid (DNA or RNA)

explanation_steps: Viruses do contain genetic material. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: E (cannot reproduce by themselves, keyed – the textbook's conclusion) and A (not made of cells, also stated on G9 p.41). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a characteristic feature of the pericardium of the heart.

options.C: Stretches with the swelling of the heart

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.50): 'The heart is covered by a tough, protective membrane called the pericardium. This membrane is both flexible and elastic. The pericardium stretches with the swelling of the heart … and then shrinks as the heart contracts.' – A, B, C, D.
'The pericardial FLUID present between the pericardium and the heart itself reduces friction' – friction is reduced by the fluid, not by the membrane itself. Answer: E.
tips: Pericardium = protective bag; pericardial fluid = lubricant.

similar_questions.stem: What is the function of the pericardial fluid?

options.B: Reduces friction between the heart and the pericardium

explanation_steps: It lubricates, reducing friction as the heart beats. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: E is keyed because the textbook attributes friction reduction to the pericardial fluid, not the pericardium itself; many books treat the fluid-filled pericardium as a whole, so a teacher may see this item as having no clearly wrong option.

questions.stem: Plants that live in dry condition show all of the following adaptations, except
explanation_steps: Xerophytes (dry-habitat plants) reduce water loss and increase water uptake: sunken stomata, small or spiny leaves, thick waxy cuticle and extensive/deep roots.
Buoyant (floating) leaves with air spaces are an adaptation of hydrophytes (water plants such as water lily). Answer: E.
tips: Xerophyte = save water; hydrophyte = float and get air.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an adaptation of water plants (hydrophytes)?

options.C: Large air spaces in stems and leaves

explanation_steps: Air spaces (aerenchyma) keep them buoyant and supply oxygen. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes

questions.stem: Answer questions 7 and 8 using the following figure. (Figure: a worm with a small head bearing a crown of hooks and round suckers, a narrow neck and a long ribbon-like body made of many segments; X points to one of the round structures on the head.) The common name of the animal in the figure is a/an
questions.image_alt: Drawing of a tapeworm: a small rounded head (scolex) with a crown of hooks on top and round cup-shaped suckers on its sides, a narrow unsegmented neck, and a long ribbon-like body of many rectangular segments. An inset arrow points from the head to a small circle marking the head's position at the end of the long chain. Label X with a line points to one of the round suckers on the head.
explanation_steps: The flat, ribbon-like body made of many segments (proglottids) and a small head (scolex) with hooks and suckers are the features of a tapeworm (Taenia), a parasitic flatworm.
Hookworm and Ascaris are round, unsegmented worms; a leech is a segmented annelid with suckers at both ends; planaria is a free-living, unsegmented flatworm. Answer: B.
tips: Scolex + proglottids = tapeworm.

similar_questions.stem: Tapeworms absorb digested food through their body surface because they
explanation_steps: As gut parasites bathed in digested food, they have no digestive system. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Using the same figure (tapeworm; X points to a round cup-shaped structure on the side of the head), the structure represented by the letter "X" is the
questions.image_alt: Drawing of a tapeworm: a small rounded head (scolex) with a crown of hooks on top and round cup-shaped suckers on its sides, a narrow unsegmented neck, and a long ribbon-like body of many rectangular segments. An inset arrow points from the head to a small circle marking the head's position at the end of the long chain. Label X with a line points to one of the round suckers on the head.
explanation_steps: The scolex carries a crown of hooks at the top and four round suckers on its sides; the pointer X touches one of the round cup-shaped structures – a sucker.
Proglottids are the body segments; the hooks are the small curved spines on top; a tapeworm has no mouth. Answer: C.
tips: Hooks and suckers anchor the tapeworm to the intestinal wall.

similar_questions.stem: The mature segments of a tapeworm that contain eggs are called
explanation_steps: Ripe proglottids full of eggs break off and pass out in faeces. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Adam's Apple is a cartilage that holds open the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.110): 'The larynx is held open with the help of cartilage. The structure called the Adam's apple is a prominent cartilage of the larynx.' Answer: B.
tips: Larynx = voice box (vocal cords); trachea is kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage.

similar_questions.stem: The vocal cords are found in the
explanation_steps: The larynx (voice box) contains the vocal cords. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following body parts is not considered as a sense organ?
explanation_steps: The five sense organs are the eye (sight), ear (hearing, balance), nose (smell), tongue (taste) and skin (touch, pressure, temperature, pain).
Skin, nose, tongue and eye are all sense organs. Answer: E.
tips: Five senses – five organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin.

similar_questions.stem: Which sense organ contains receptors for heat, cold and pressure?
explanation_steps: The skin has touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain receptors. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 7.1 The sense organs – introduction; 7.1.1 The skin

questions.stem: One can find lymphatic tissues in the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.85, 91–92): the lymphatic system includes lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, tonsils, spleen and thymus gland; these organs contain lymphatic tissue.
The lungs are respiratory organs and are not listed as lymphatic organs. Answer: E.
tips: Lymphoid organs: lymph nodes, tonsils, adenoids, spleen, thymus (and Peyer's patches in the gut).

similar_questions.stem: Which lymphatic organ filters blood and destroys old red blood cells?
explanation_steps: The spleen filters blood. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 Components of the lymphatic system; lymphatic tissue

questions.stem: The systemic circuit extends

options.A: from the heart to the lungs.
options.B: from the heart to the coronary arteries only.
options.C: from the heart to the body's organs and tissues.
options.D: from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver.
options.E: from the heart to the kidneys.

explanation_steps: Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → lungs → left atrium.
Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → all body organs and tissues → venae cavae → right atrium. Answer: C.
B, D and E are only parts of the systemic circuit (coronary, hepatic portal and renal circulations).
tips: Pulmonary = lungs; systemic = the whole body.

similar_questions.stem: Blood in the pulmonary veins is carried from the
explanation_steps: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3 Circulation routes – pulmonary and systemic circulation

questions.stem: Endoskeleton

options.A: is under the muscles and soft tissues.
options.C: becomes impractically heavy as organisms increase in size.

explanation_steps: An endoskeleton is an internal skeleton (bone and cartilage) lying beneath the muscles and soft tissues; it grows with the body.
B–E are disadvantages of an EXOSKELETON (textbook Table 3.1): it limits size, becomes too heavy in large animals, does not grow and must be moulted, leaving the animal vulnerable. Answer: A.
tips: Endo = inside and growing; exo = outside, must moult.

similar_questions.stem: Which animal has an exoskeleton?
explanation_steps: Arthropods such as grasshoppers have a chitin exoskeleton. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is incorrect about reproduction? It

options.A: produces new individuals from their parents.
options.B: is carried out by all organisms.
options.C: is a process whereby organisms give rise to others of the same type.
options.D: ensures the continuity of life and/or the species.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.25): 'Reproduction is a biological process in which new individuals are produced from their parent(s). It is a life process that is carried out by all organisms. It is the process whereby organisms give rise to others of the same type. Reproduction is important in ensuring the continuity of life and/or the species.'
Statements A–D are all taken from the textbook, so none is incorrect. Answer: E.
(Strictly, some individuals – mules, worker bees – never reproduce, but at the level of species the textbook statement holds.)
tips: When every option matches the textbook sentence by sentence, choose 'None of the above'.

similar_questions.stem: Asexual reproduction differs from sexual reproduction because it

options.C: produces offspring identical to the parent

explanation_steps: One parent, no gametes, genetically identical offspring. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true?

options.A: Kidneys excrete urea and mineral salts.
options.D: Liver destroys old red blood cells.

explanation_steps: Kidneys excrete urea, salts and water (urine); lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour; skin excretes sweat; the liver breaks down old red blood cells (bile pigments) and makes urea.
Lungs do not excrete oxygen as a waste (O₂ is absorbed) and do not expel ions. Answer: E.
tips: Excretory organ → product: kidney → urine; lungs → CO₂ + H₂O; skin → sweat; liver → bile pigments, urea.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ converts excess amino acids into urea?
explanation_steps: Deamination and urea formation take place in the liver. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Abnormal hormonal secretion of Pituitary Gland results in
explanation_steps: Oversecretion of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary in childhood causes gigantism (dwarfism if undersecreted; acromegaly in adults).
Cretinism, goitre and myxoedema are thyroid disorders; diabetes mellitus is a pancreas (insulin) disorder. Answer: A.
tips: Pituitary → GH → gigantism/dwarfism; thyroid → thyroxine → cretinism, myxoedema, goitre; pancreas → insulin → diabetes.

similar_questions.stem: Cretinism in children is caused by
explanation_steps: Thyroxine deficiency from birth causes cretinism. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following scientists contributed in the formulation of the Cell Theory, except
explanation_steps: Robert Hooke (1665) discovered and named cells; van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells; Schleiden (1838, plants) and Schwann (1839, animals) stated that all living things are made of cells.
Carl Linnaeus developed binomial nomenclature and classification, not the cell theory. Answer: A.
tips: Linnaeus = father of taxonomy.

similar_questions.stem: Who concluded that all animals are made of cells?
explanation_steps: Schwann (1839) – animals; Schleiden (1838) – plants. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The Carbon Cycle involves
explanation_steps: Carbon moves from the air into organisms by photosynthesis and returns to the air by respiration, decomposition of dead organisms and combustion of fuels (including industrial emissions). Answer: E.
tips: Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decay and burning add CO₂.

similar_questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
explanation_steps: Plants fix CO₂ into sugars. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Nucleic acids are found in all the following, except
explanation_steps: Every living cell (bacteria, fungi, protozoa) contains DNA and RNA.
Viruses contain either DNA or RNA inside the capsid (textbook G9 p.41: 'viruses do have their own nucleic acid').
All four contain nucleic acids. Answer: E.
tips: Nucleic acids = genetic material of every organism and virus.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these contains RNA but no DNA?
explanation_steps: Retroviruses such as HIV have RNA genomes. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The growing points of plants are found at the tip of the
explanation_steps: Growth in length happens at apical meristems – regions of actively dividing cells at the tips of stems (shoot apex) and roots (root apex, protected by the root cap). Answer: E.
tips: Apical meristems → primary growth (length); lateral meristems (cambium) → growth in thickness.

similar_questions.stem: The tissue responsible for increase in the girth (thickness) of a stem is
explanation_steps: Lateral meristem (cambium) gives secondary growth. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Homeostasis can be achieved by getting
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.84): 'Proper exercise, a well balanced diet, proper sleeping patterns and taking adequate rest may also help to achieve homeostatic balance.' Answer: E.
tips: Healthy lifestyle supports the body's feedback systems.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ is the main control centre for homeostasis of body temperature?
explanation_steps: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and triggers responses. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Cellular respiration is involved in the
explanation_steps: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and converts its chemical energy into ATP – an energy conversion that occurs in all living cells, including plant cells (day and night).
Energy storage (starch, glycogen, fat) is not respiration; viruses have no metabolism. Answer: A.
tips: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases/converts it.

similar_questions.stem: The energy-carrying molecule produced in cellular respiration is
explanation_steps: Respiration transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: During osmosis, the movement of water across a membrane is dependent on the
explanation_steps: Osmosis is the movement of water from a weaker (dilute) to a stronger (concentrated) solution through a semi-permeable membrane.
What drives it is the difference in solute concentration on the two sides (which sets the water concentration); it is passive – no carrier proteins or energy needed. Answer: B.
Note: the textbook speaks of 'water concentration'; A (solvent concentration) says the same thing from the other side, but 'solute concentration' is the standard answer.
tips: Water moves toward the side with MORE solute.

similar_questions.stem: A red blood cell placed in pure water will
explanation_steps: Water enters the cell, which has the higher solute concentration. Answer: B.

questions.stem: During the dark reaction of photosynthesis,

options.B: light energy is converted to chemical energy.

explanation_steps: Light reaction: chlorophyll traps light, water is split, O₂ is released and energy is stored in ATP/NADPH.
Dark (light-independent) reaction: CO₂ is fixed and reduced using that energy to make glucose. Answer: A.
tips: Light reaction → O₂ + ATP; dark reaction → sugar.

similar_questions.stem: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from
explanation_steps: Photolysis of water in the light reaction. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is incorrect about the organisms that belong to the kingdom Protista?

options.B: Most are unicellular but sometimes they join together.
options.C: Some make their own food while others feed on other organisms.
options.D: Protozoa, algae and slime molds are members of the kingdom.
options.E: Some members of the kingdom are single-celled prokaryotes.

explanation_steps: Protists are simple eukaryotes, mostly unicellular (some colonial), autotrophic (algae) or heterotrophic (protozoa), and include protozoa, algae and slime moulds.
Prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria) belong to kingdom Monera, not Protista. Answer: E.
tips: Monera = prokaryotes; all other kingdoms are eukaryotes.

similar_questions.stem: Amoeba belongs to the kingdom
explanation_steps: Amoeba is a protozoan (animal-like protist). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is considered as a "vestigial organ"?
explanation_steps: Vestigial organs are dwarfed and generally useless organs whose homologues are functional in related organisms (textbook G12 p.72).
The human (vermiform) appendix is the reduced remains of a caecum that is large and functional in herbivores. Answer: D.
tips: Human vestigial organs: appendix, coccyx (tail bone), ear muscles, nictitating membrane, wisdom teeth.

similar_questions.stem: Vestigial organs are evidence for evolution from
explanation_steps: Vestigial organs are studied in comparative anatomy. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 Evidence of evolution – comparative anatomy (vestigial organs)

questions.stem: Blood returning to the heart from the body organs enters into the

options.B: right atrium through the vena cava.
options.C: left ventricle by the pulmonary artery.
options.D: right ventricle by the pulmonary vein.

explanation_steps: Deoxygenated blood from the body returns through the superior and inferior venae cavae into the right atrium.
The aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle; pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Answer: B.
tips: Right side = body blood (deoxygenated); left side = lung blood (oxygenated).

similar_questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the body?
explanation_steps: The aorta leaves the left ventricle. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms of scurvy is incorrect?
explanation_steps: Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C. Textbook Table 1.3 (G10 p.17) lists: bleeding of gums and mouth, anaemia, poor healing of wounds, bleeding under the skin.
Delayed blood clotting is a symptom of vitamin K deficiency, not scurvy. Answer: A.
tips: Vitamin C → scurvy (gums); vitamin K → clotting; vitamin D → rickets; vitamin A → night blindness.

similar_questions.stem: Lack of vitamin D in children causes
explanation_steps: Vitamin D is needed for calcium absorption; deficiency → soft bones (rickets). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the adaptation of organisms?

options.A: Avoidance reduces the impact of the stress.
options.B: Tolerance enables organisms to live under stressful conditions.
options.C: Escape enables organisms to avoid stressful circumstances.
options.E: Adaptation increases the fitness of organisms.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.141): 'Adaptation is hereditary and thus passed from one generation to the next.' Adaptation mechanisms are avoidance (reduces the impact of stress), tolerance (lets the organism live under stress) and escape.
D contradicts the textbook. Answer: D.
tips: Adaptations are inherited features shaped by natural selection.

similar_questions.stem: A desert plant that completes its life cycle quickly during the short rainy season shows
explanation_steps: It escapes the drought by finishing its life cycle before it. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment

questions.stem: In which of the following products are the largest amounts of nitrogen excreted from a mammalian body?
explanation_steps: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and the nitrogen is converted to urea, which the kidneys excrete in urine.
Sweat contains only a little urea; breath contains CO₂ and water; faeces are mostly undigested material (egestion). Answer: C.
tips: Mammals excrete nitrogen mainly as urea in urine.

similar_questions.stem: The main nitrogenous waste of mammals is
explanation_steps: Mammals are ureotelic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In the process of bread making, which molecule causes the bread to rise?
explanation_steps: Yeast in the dough ferments sugar: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (+ energy).
Bubbles of carbon dioxide are trapped in the dough and make it rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking. Answer: C.
tips: Bread: CO₂ matters; beer/wine: ethanol matters.

similar_questions.stem: Alcoholic fermentation by yeast produces
explanation_steps: Anaerobic respiration in yeast gives ethanol + CO₂. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: The physical barriers that form part of the human immune system are the

options.B: bone marrow and the mucosal membrane.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.101–102): a pathogen must bypass the physical components of the immune system – the skin and mucus (mucous membranes) – and resist chemical defences (tears, mucus secretions, saliva).
Tears and saliva are chemical defences; antibodies and bone marrow belong to specific immunity. Answer: A.
tips: Physical barriers: skin, mucous membranes (with cilia). Chemical: tears, saliva, stomach acid.

similar_questions.stem: Lysozyme in tears is an example of a
explanation_steps: Tears contain lysozyme that chemically destroys bacteria. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1 Innate immunity – physical and chemical barriers

questions.stem: The lymph fluid consists of the following substances, except
explanation_steps: Lymph is tissue fluid collected by lymph vessels: water, dissolved nutrients and wastes, absorbed (digested) fat from the lacteals and many lymphocytes.
Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are too large to leave the capillaries, so lymph contains none. Answer: D.
tips: Lymph = plasma-like fluid + white cells (lymphocytes), no red cells.

similar_questions.stem: Fats absorbed in the small intestine first enter the
explanation_steps: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the lacteals. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The semilunar valves prevent blood from flowing backwards into the
explanation_steps: The aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves lie at the exits of the ventricles.
When the ventricles relax, blood tries to flow back from the aorta and pulmonary artery and closes these valves, preventing backflow into the ventricles. Answer: B.
The atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves prevent backflow into the atria.
tips: AV valves protect the atria; semilunar valves protect the ventricles.

similar_questions.stem: The bicuspid (mitral) valve is found between the
explanation_steps: The bicuspid valve is on the left side between atrium and ventricle. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the followings are the main functions of hormones, except
explanation_steps: Hormones' main functions are usually listed as: reproduction and sexual differentiation; development and growth; maintenance of the internal environment; regulation of metabolism (energy production). The textbook (G11 p.2) says the endocrine system regulates behaviour, growth, development, tissue function, metabolism, sexual function and reproduction.

A, B, D and E (metabolism – thyroxine raises the metabolic rate) fit this list. Maintaining body temperature is mainly a nervous (hypothalamic) reflex function and is not named as a main hormone function. Answer: C (keyed as the setter's probable intent).
tips: Main hormone functions: growth/development, reproduction, metabolism, internal environment.

similar_questions.stem: The hormone that increases the basal metabolic rate is
explanation_steps: Thyroxine from the thyroid raises the metabolic rate. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 The endocrine glands – role of the endocrine system

questions.review_flag: No option is clearly outside the functions of hormones: body temperature (C) is part of the internal environment and hormones such as thyroxine do raise metabolic rate (E). C is keyed as the likely intent; E is also accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an endocrine gland?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.2): 'The main endocrine glands in the human body are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, islets of Langerhans (pancreas), thymus, pineal and sex glands.'
The hypothalamus is a part of the brain (below the thalamus) that controls the pituitary; it is not listed as an endocrine gland. Answer: A.
Caution: the hypothalamus does contain neurosecretory cells that make ADH and oxytocin, so it is often called a neuro-endocrine organ.
tips: Pancreas = both exocrine (enzymes) and endocrine (insulin, glucagon).

similar_questions.stem: Which gland is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland?
explanation_steps: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes (duct) and insulin/glucagon (blood). Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 The endocrine glands; 1.1.1 hypothalamus and pituitary

questions.review_flag: The hypothalamus is keyed because the textbook's list of main endocrine glands (G11 p.2) omits it, but it secretes hormones (ADH, oxytocin, releasing hormones) and many books call it an endocrine organ.

questions.stem: A thin transparent membrane that covers the front of the eyeball in humans is called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.147): 'The front of the eyeball is covered by a thin, transparent membrane, the conjunctiva. The conjunctiva protects the cornea against damage from friction.'
The cornea is the transparent front part of the sclera (the window of the eye) lying beneath the conjunctiva. Answer: A.
tips: Conjunctiva = protective skin over the cornea; conjunctivitis = 'pink eye'.

similar_questions.stem: The coloured part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil is the
explanation_steps: The iris contains muscles that change pupil size. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following cell types stop reproducing shortly after birth?
explanation_steps: Mature nerve cells (neurons) lose the ability to divide; their numbers are essentially fixed soon after birth, which is why nerve damage heals poorly.
White blood cells are continually produced from bone marrow stem cells; liver cells can divide to regenerate the liver. Answer: C.
Brain cells (E) are mostly neurons and heart muscle cells (B) also practically stop dividing after birth, so these are defensible too.
tips: Cells that do not divide after maturity: neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle fibres.

similar_questions.stem: Which cells are produced continuously throughout life?
explanation_steps: Red cells live about 120 days and are constantly replaced by the bone marrow. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook describes neuron structure but does not state when cell division stops; answer based on standard biology.

questions.review_flag: Ambiguous: nerve cells (C, keyed), brain cells (E, mostly neurons) and heart muscle cells (B) all essentially stop dividing after birth, and the textbook does not address this. C, E and B accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves are branched out of the spinal cord?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.176–177): 12 pairs of cranial nerves branch from the brain and 31 pairs of spinal nerves from the spinal cord (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: How many pairs of cranial nerves arise from the human brain?
explanation_steps: 12 pairs of cranial nerves. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 8.3 The peripheral nervous system – spinal nerves

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the umbilical cord? It

options.A: is supplied with arteries and veins.
options.B: connects the placenta and the embryo.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.41–42): 'The placenta is connected to the body of the embryo by a long, cord-like structure called the umbilical cord. The cord is supplied with arteries and veins.'
Food and oxygen pass from the mother through the placenta and umbilical vein to the embryo; wastes (CO₂, urea) return through the umbilical arteries. All four statements are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Umbilical vein → oxygenated, food-rich blood to the fetus; umbilical arteries → wastes to the placenta.

similar_questions.stem: Exchange of materials between mother and fetus takes place in the
explanation_steps: Maternal and fetal blood exchange materials across the placenta without mixing. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The human axial skeleton includes
explanation_steps: Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum (breastbone).
Humerus (upper arm), carpus (wrist), femur (thigh) and fibula (lower leg) belong to the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles). Answer: A.
tips: Axial = the body's axis; appendicular = appendages (limbs) and girdles.

similar_questions.stem: Which bone belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
explanation_steps: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Muscles have no function in the
explanation_steps: Respiratory system: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles ventilate the lungs. Digestive system: smooth muscle moves food by peristalsis. Circulatory system: cardiac muscle pumps blood and smooth muscle controls vessel diameter.
The endocrine system works through hormones secreted by glands, not by muscle action. Answer: D.
tips: Three muscle types: skeletal (movement, breathing), smooth (gut, vessels, airways), cardiac (heart).

similar_questions.stem: Which muscle type is found in the walls of the stomach and intestines?
explanation_steps: Smooth (involuntary) muscle causes peristalsis. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The hormone that targets mammary glands is
explanation_steps: Prolactin (anterior pituitary) stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk; oxytocin (posterior pituitary) causes the mammary glands to eject (let down) milk and the uterus to contract.
Both hormones target the mammary glands. Answer: E.
tips: Prolactin → milk production; oxytocin → milk ejection.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates contraction of the uterus during childbirth?
explanation_steps: Oxytocin causes uterine contractions. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 The pituitary gland – prolactin and oxytocin

questions.stem: Primary sexual characters are manifested by
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.26): primary sexual characteristics are the structures that make an organism male or female – the reproductive (genital) organs: testes, penis; ovaries, uterus, vagina.
Anatomical, behavioural and mental changes at puberty (voice, body hair, breasts) are secondary sexual characteristics. Answer: A.
tips: Primary = sex organs present from birth; secondary = puberty changes.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a secondary sexual characteristic of males?
explanation_steps: The voice deepens at puberty under testosterone. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 Puberty – primary and secondary sexual characteristics

questions.stem: The vascular system of a plant includes the
explanation_steps: Vascular (conducting) tissue consists of xylem (water and minerals up from the roots) and phloem (food/sugars from the leaves).
Epidermis is dermal tissue and parenchyma is ground tissue. Answer: E.
tips: Xylem – water up; phloem – food both ways.

similar_questions.stem: Which tissue transports sugar made in the leaves to other parts of the plant?
explanation_steps: Phloem translocates organic food. Answer: B.

questions.stem: If two birds of the same population are not attracted to each other through singing, this isolation is referred as
explanation_steps: Courtship song is a behaviour; when it no longer attracts mates, mating is prevented.
Textbook (G12 p.81): 'Behavioural isolation: Behaviour may have changed so much that mating is prevented.' Answer: E.
tips: Isolating mechanisms: behavioural (courtship), seasonal (time), habitat (place), mechanical (organs), gametic/zygotic mortality.

similar_questions.stem: Two populations of frogs breed in different months of the year. This is
explanation_steps: Different breeding seasons = seasonal isolation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In sexually reproducing organisms, a source of genetic variation that introduces new genetic combination into a population is known as
explanation_steps: Genetic recombination – crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis plus random fertilisation – reshuffles existing alleles into new combinations in each generation of sexually reproducing organisms.
Mutation produces new alleles (new genes) rather than new combinations; isolation and gametic/zygotic mortality reduce gene flow. Answer: B.
tips: Mutation = new alleles; recombination = new combinations of alleles.

similar_questions.stem: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during
explanation_steps: Homologues pair and exchange segments in prophase I. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.4 Sources of genetic variation – genetic recombination

questions.stem: Why is it important to maintain a constant body temperature?

options.A: To stop the multiplication of bacteria in the body
options.B: To have enough energy to move
options.C: To maintain optimum temperature for enzymes to function

explanation_steps: All metabolic reactions are catalysed by enzymes, which work best at an optimum temperature (about 37 °C in humans); at low temperatures they are slow and at high temperatures they are denatured.
Keeping body temperature constant keeps enzymes working at their optimum. Answer: C.
tips: Homeostasis protects enzymes: constant temperature and pH.

similar_questions.stem: What happens to most human enzymes at 60 °C?

options.B: They are denatured and stop working

explanation_steps: High temperatures change the enzyme's shape (denaturation). Answer: B.

questions.stem: What is the best definition of homeostasis?

options.B: Maintenance of a constant internal environment
options.D: Taking in oxygen and getting rid of carbon dioxide

explanation_steps: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant (stable) internal environment – temperature, water, salts, glucose, pH – despite changes outside.
A is excretion, C only one part of homeostasis (thermoregulation), D gas exchange. Answer: B.
tips: Homeo = same, stasis = standing still.

similar_questions.stem: Regulation of the water and salt content of the body is called
explanation_steps: Osmoregulation keeps water/solute balance. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A nucleoside consists of
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.2): 'The base-sugar unit is called a nucleoside … The base-sugar-phosphate unit is therefore called a nucleotide.' Answer: B.
tips: Nucleoside + phosphate = nucleotide.

similar_questions.stem: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation_steps: RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Answer: E.

questions.stem: The dominant allele 'A' causes seeds of maize to be coloured, whereas the recessive allele 'a' causes seeds to be colourless. From the cross Aa × Aa, what fraction of the produced seeds are colourless?
explanation_steps: Each Aa parent gives A or a gametes with probability ½.
Punnett square: AA (¼), Aa (½), aa (¼).
Only aa seeds are colourless: 1/4. Answer: C.
tips: Monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes: 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

similar_questions.stem: In peas, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). What fraction of the offspring of Tt × tt are dwarf?
explanation_steps: Tt × tt → Tt : tt = 1 : 1, so ½ are dwarf. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the function of the tRNA molecule? It

options.A: contains chemical information known as genes.
options.B: contains transcribed information needed to build a protein.
options.D: translates the language of nucleotides into that of amino acids.

explanation_steps: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon – so tRNA 'translates' the nucleotide language into amino acids.
Genes are in DNA (A); mRNA carries the transcribed message (B); rRNA forms the ribosome, which is the 'bench' for translation (C, E). Answer: D.
tips: DNA = master copy; mRNA = message; tRNA = translator/adaptor; rRNA = workbench.

similar_questions.stem: The mRNA codon AUG pairs with the tRNA anticodon
explanation_steps: A–U, U–A, G–C: anticodon UAC. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Meiotic cell division

options.C: is found in all sexually reproducing organisms.
options.D: produces cells with haploid number of chromosomes.

explanation_steps: Meiosis has two successive divisions (meiosis I and II) and produces four daughter cells, each with the haploid (n) number of chromosomes.
It occurs in all sexually reproducing organisms to form gametes (or spores). All statements are true. Answer: E.
tips: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 diploid identical cells. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 haploid varied cells.

similar_questions.stem: A cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. Each daughter cell has
explanation_steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: 23. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about amino acids?

options.A: They are the building blocks of polysaccharides.
options.B: All amino acids contain the same number of carbon atoms.
options.C: All amino acids contain amino group.
options.D: Amino group of amino acids contains carbon and nitrogen elements.
options.E: There are more than 120 amino acids in nature.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.7): amino acids are the building blocks of proteins (not polysaccharides); 'there are 20 amino acids in nature'; 'all amino acids contain' an amino group (–NH₂) and a carboxyl group (–COOH).
Amino acids differ in their side chains, so their carbon numbers differ; the amino group (–NH₂) contains nitrogen and hydrogen, not carbon. Answer: C.
tips: General amino acid: H₂N–CH(R)–COOH.

similar_questions.stem: Two amino acids join by a
explanation_steps: The –COOH of one reacts with –NH₂ of the next (condensation) forming a peptide bond. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following events does not happen in response to loss of body moisture?

options.A: Receptors in hypothalamus change in blood concentration.
options.B: ADH release from the posterior pituitary increases.
options.C: ADH flows to nephrons of the kidneys.
options.D: Decreased water retention and reabsorption results.

explanation_steps: When the body loses water, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the more concentrated blood (A); more ADH is released from the posterior pituitary (B) and carried in the blood to the kidney nephrons (C).
ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so MORE water is reabsorbed and retained, and blood water rises back to normal (E).
'Decreased water retention and reabsorption' is the opposite of what happens. Answer: D.
tips: Dehydrated → ADH ↑ → water reabsorption ↑ → small volume of concentrated urine.

similar_questions.stem: After drinking a large volume of water, a person produces

options.B: more dilute urine because ADH falls

explanation_steps: Excess water lowers ADH release, so less water is reabsorbed. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Interspecific relationship mainly involves
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.89): intra-specific relations (same species) include co-operation and competition, such as the division of territory and hierarchical organisation.

'Inter-specific relations are interactions between different species. The most significant relation is that of predation.' Others: parasitism, disease and competition between species sharing a niche. Answer: D.
tips: Intra = within one species; inter = between species.

similar_questions.stem: Two male lions fighting over a territory is an example of
explanation_steps: Same species competing = intraspecific. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Acid rain results from the pollution of
explanation_steps: Burning fossil fuels releases sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into the AIR; these dissolve in rain water to form sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as acid rain.
Acid rain then damages water, soil and plants, but its cause is air pollution. Answer: B.
tips: SO₂ + NOₓ (from factories and vehicles) + rain → acid rain.

similar_questions.stem: The main gases responsible for acid rain are
explanation_steps: SO₂ and NOₓ form H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ in rain. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 Ecosystem – human impact on the environment
textbook_ref.note: Acid rain is not described in the extracted Biology textbook text; answered from standard environmental science.

questions.stem: Referring to evolution, an organism that produces many offspring at a time is better than the one that produces few offspring at a time. This theory is best described by
explanation_steps: Darwin's theory of natural selection begins with overproduction: organisms produce far more offspring than can survive, leading to a struggle for existence and survival of the fittest (textbook G12 p.63).
Lamarckism is about use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters; Mendel's work is about inheritance, not evolution. Answer: A.
Neo-Darwinism (D) keeps natural selection but adds genetics; the overproduction idea itself is Darwin's.
tips: Darwin: overproduction → variation → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → origin of species.

similar_questions.stem: 'The giraffe got its long neck by stretching to reach leaves and passed this on to its offspring.' This explanation is
explanation_steps: Inheritance of acquired characteristics is Lamarck's idea. Answer: B.

questions.stem: From the cross Bb × Bb, where B is dominant to b, how many different genotypes are produced among the offspring and in what proportion are they expected?
explanation_steps: Bb × Bb → BB : Bb : bb = 1 : 2 : 1.
That is three different genotypes in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio (the 3 : 1 ratio is for phenotypes). Answer: B.
tips: Genotypic ratio 1:2:1; phenotypic ratio 3:1.

similar_questions.stem: How many different phenotypes result from Bb × Bb with complete dominance?
explanation_steps: Dominant and recessive phenotypes only: 2 (ratio 3:1). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following plasma components corresponds with its function?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.67) lists the functions of plasma constituents: transporting nutrients, gases and vitamins; regulating fluid and electrolyte balance; maintaining a favourable pH; helping to fight disease (globulins contain antibodies); proper clotting of blood (fibrinogen).

Fibrinogen – blood clotting (C) and globulin – fighting disease (B) are both paired this way in the textbook, and water is the transport medium for nutrients (D). pH is maintained mainly by buffers and plasma proteins, so A is the weakest pairing.
The item has more than one correct option; C is keyed as the most specific textbook pairing.
tips: Plasma proteins: albumin (osmotic balance), globulins (antibodies), fibrinogen (clotting).

similar_questions.stem: Which plasma protein is converted into fibrin during blood clotting?
explanation_steps: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Defective item: B (globulin – fighting disease), C (fibrinogen – clotting) and D (water – transport of nutrients) are all correct pairings (textbook G10 p.67). C keyed; B and D also accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: An object is observed under a microscope using an eyepiece (ocular) of 10X and the low power objective (4X). Calculate the total magnification power. (1 point)
explanation_steps: A compound light microscope magnifies twice: first by the objective lens, then by the eyepiece (textbook G9 p.6).
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification = 10 × 4 = 40.
The image is 40 times larger than the object (40X).
marking_points: Correct working 10 × 4 (½ point) and answer 40X (½ point)
40X alone: full point
tips: Multiply, never add, the two magnifications.

similar_questions.stem: A student uses a 15X eyepiece with the 40X objective. What is the total magnification?
explanation_steps: 15 × 40 = 600, so the total magnification is 600X.

questions.stem: The three main feeding trophic levels are 2.1 ____, 2.2 ____, 2.3 ____. (1.5 points)
questions.answer: 2.1 Producers (green plants); 2.2 primary consumers (herbivores); 2.3 secondary consumers (carnivores). Tertiary consumers or decomposers may be accepted.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.101): organisms that make their own food (green plants) are producers; organisms that feed on others are consumers.
Energy passes from producers → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers (carnivores) → tertiary consumers.
Decomposers break down dead matter from every level.
marking_points: ½ point each: producers; primary consumers/herbivores; secondary consumers/carnivores
Accept tertiary consumers or decomposers in place of one consumer level (teacher's discretion)
tips: Trophic = feeding; level 1 is always the producers.

similar_questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, name the trophic level of (a) the grasshopper and (b) the snake.
explanation_steps: Grass = producer, grasshopper = primary, frog = secondary, snake = tertiary consumer.

questions.stem: Give at least two examples of 3.1 omnivorous animals (a, b) and 3.2 poikilothermic vertebrates (a, b). (2 points)
questions.answer: 3.1 Human, pig (also bear, rat, chicken, baboon). 3.2 Fish (e.g. tilapia), amphibians (frog, toad), reptiles (lizard, snake, crocodile, tortoise).

subparts.question: Two omnivorous animals
subparts.answer: Human and pig (or bear, rat, chicken)

subparts.question: Two poikilothermic vertebrates
subparts.answer: Fish and frog (or any reptile such as a lizard or snake)
steps: Fish, amphibians and reptiles are cold-blooded.

explanation_steps: Omnivores eat both plant and animal food; they have teeth for both biting and grinding (textbook G9 p.111). Examples: humans, pigs, bears, rats.

Poikilothermic (cold-blooded) animals cannot keep their body temperature constant; it changes with the environment. Among vertebrates these are fishes, amphibians and reptiles (G9 p.103–105). Birds and mammals are homeothermic.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct example (four examples)
3.2: do not accept birds, mammals or invertebrates
tips: Poikilothermic vertebrates: 'FAR' – Fish, Amphibians, Reptiles.

similar_questions.stem: Give two examples each of (a) herbivorous mammals and (b) homeothermic (warm-blooded) vertebrate classes.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Cow, goat, sheep, camel, rabbit (any two); (b) birds and mammals.
explanation_steps: Herbivores eat only plants; only birds and mammals keep a constant body temperature.

questions.stem: What are the two organ systems of a plant? 4.1 ____ 4.2 ____ (1 point)
explanation_steps: A flowering plant body has two organ systems: the shoot system above ground (stem, leaves, buds, flowers, fruits) and the root system usually below ground (main root, lateral roots).
marking_points: ½ point each: shoot system; root system
tips: Shoot = above ground; root = below ground.

similar_questions.stem: To which organ system do (a) flowers and (b) root hairs belong?
explanation_steps: Flowers grow on the shoot; root hairs are part of the root system.

questions.stem: What is the function of the epiglottis in the human body? (1 point)
questions.answer: During swallowing the epiglottis closes (covers) the opening of the trachea (glottis), so food and liquid pass into the oesophagus and not into the windpipe.
explanation_steps: When food is swallowed the larynx rises and the epiglottis, a flap of cartilage, folds over the glottis (G10 p.33–34).
This prevents choking by guiding the bolus into the oesophagus.
marking_points: Closes/covers the trachea (glottis/windpipe) during swallowing (½)
so food goes into the oesophagus / prevents choking (½)
tips: Epiglottis = 'lid' over the windpipe.

similar_questions.stem: Why can we not breathe and swallow at the same time?
similar_questions.answer: Because during swallowing the epiglottis closes the entrance of the trachea.
explanation_steps: The air passage is temporarily blocked while the bolus passes the pharynx.

questions.stem:
Fill in the table. (2.5 points)
Organelle – Function
Ribosome – 6.1 ____
6.2 ____ – Cellular respiration
Nucleus – 6.3 ____
6.4 ____ – Cleaning
Chloroplast – 6.5 ____
questions.answer: 6.1 Protein synthesis; 6.2 mitochondrion; 6.3 controls all cell activities (contains DNA/genetic material); 6.4 lysosome; 6.5 photosynthesis.

subparts.question: Function of nucleus
subparts.answer: Controls cell activities / carries genetic information

explanation_steps: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration and are the 'power house' of the cell (G9 p.13).
The nucleus contains chromosomes (DNA) and controls cell activities.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and foreign material – the cell's cleaners.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
marking_points: ½ point each of the five blanks

similar_questions.stem: Name the organelle that (a) packages and secretes proteins, (b) regulates what enters and leaves the cell.
explanation_steps: The Golgi modifies and packages products; the selectively permeable membrane controls transport.

questions.stem: Agglutination occurs due to a reaction between 7.1 ____ and 7.2 ____ carried in the plasma of human blood. (1 point)
questions.answer: 7.1 Antigens (agglutinogens) on the red blood cells; 7.2 antibodies (agglutinins) in the plasma.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.77): red cells carry antigens (agglutinogens A and/or B); plasma carries antibodies (agglutinins anti-A, anti-B).
When an antigen meets its matching antibody (e.g. A with anti-A), the red cells clump together – agglutination.
marking_points: ½ point each: antigen/agglutinogen; antibody/agglutinin (either order)
tips: Antigen on the cell, antibody in the plasma.

similar_questions.stem: Which antigens and antibodies does a person of blood group B have?
similar_questions.answer: Antigen B on red cells; anti-A antibodies in the plasma.
explanation_steps: A person never carries antibodies against his own antigens.

questions.stem: Identify the type of joints indicated in the figure (8.1 skull, 8.2 hip, 8.3 knee). (1.5 points)
questions.image_alt: Human skeleton with three circled joints: 8.1 at the top of the skull, 8.2 at the hip, 8.3 at the knee.
questions.answer: 8.1 Immovable (fixed/suture) joint; 8.2 ball-and-socket joint; 8.3 hinge joint.
explanation_steps: 8.1 points to the skull: the cranial bones are joined by sutures – immovable (fixed) joints (G11 p.69).
8.2 points to the hip: the head of the femur fits into the socket of the pelvis – a ball-and-socket joint allowing movement in all directions (G11 p.70).
8.3 points to the knee: a hinge joint allowing movement in one plane only (flexion and extension) (G11 p.68–69).
marking_points: ½ point each: immovable/fixed/suture; ball-and-socket; hinge
tips: Shoulder and hip = ball-and-socket; elbow, knee, fingers = hinge; atlas–axis = pivot; skull = immovable.

similar_questions.stem: Name the type of joint found at (a) the shoulder, (b) the elbow, (c) between the atlas and axis.
explanation_steps: See the joint types in the textbook.

questions.stem: Define the following terms. 9.1 Transpiration 9.2 Transcription (1 point)
questions.answer: 9.1 Transpiration: the loss of water in the form of vapour from a living plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. 9.2 Transcription: the synthesis of an RNA (mRNA) molecule complementary to one strand of DNA.

subparts.question: Transpiration
subparts.answer: Loss of water vapour from the plant (leaves/stomata)

subparts.question: Transcription
subparts.answer: Making RNA from a DNA template

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.132): 'The loss of water in vapor form from a living plant through the leaves' is transpiration.
Textbook (G12 p.10): a cell produces a complementary copy of one strand of a DNA molecule by synthesising RNA – transcription – the first step of protein synthesis.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct definition
tips: Transpiration – plants and water; transcription – DNA → RNA; translation – RNA → protein.

similar_questions.stem: Define translation.
similar_questions.answer: Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide (protein) on ribosomes using the codon sequence of mRNA, with tRNA bringing the amino acids.
explanation_steps: mRNA codons are read by tRNA anticodons.

questions.stem: List the necessary steps of the lytic cycle (phase) of a bacteriophage. (2 points)
questions.answer: 1. Attachment of the phage to the bacterial cell surface; 2. penetration (injection) of the phage nucleic acid; 3. replication – synthesis of new phage DNA and proteins, and maturation; 4. assembly of new phages, followed by lysis (bursting) of the cell and release.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.42, Fig. 1.15): a. attachment to the cell surface; b. the nucleic acid of the phage penetrates; c. maturation of the phage; d. the phage is assembled and bursts out of the cell to infect other cells.
During the middle stage the host's machinery is used to copy the viral nucleic acid and make capsid proteins.
marking_points: ½ point for each step in the correct order: attachment; penetration/injection; replication/maturation; assembly and lysis/release
Accept five-step versions (attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, release)
tips: Attach → Inject → Replicate → Assemble → Lyse (A-I-R-A-L).

similar_questions.stem: How does the lysogenic cycle differ from the lytic cycle?
similar_questions.answer: In the lysogenic cycle the viral DNA joins the host chromosome and is copied with it without killing the cell (dormant); in the lytic cycle new viruses are made at once and the cell bursts.
explanation_steps: The lysogenic virus may later switch to the lytic cycle.

questions.stem:
The following cycle represents the oxygen cycle. Fill the missing parts in the cycle (11.1, 11.2, 11.3). (1.5 points)
(Diagram: solar energy → Photosynthesis → Glucose and 11.1 → 11.2; 11.2 gives H₂O and 11.3, which return to Photosynthesis.)
questions.image_alt: Cycle diagram: solar energy arrow into a Photosynthesis box; arrows from Photosynthesis to Glucose and to box 11.1, both pointing to box 11.2; from 11.2 arrows to H2O and box 11.3, which point back to Photosynthesis.
explanation_steps: Photosynthesis uses solar energy, CO₂ and H₂O to make glucose and release oxygen (11.1).
Glucose and O₂ are used in cellular respiration (11.2): C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy.
Respiration returns H₂O and CO₂ (11.3) to photosynthesis, completing the cycle.
marking_points: ½ point each: O₂; respiration; CO₂
tips: Photosynthesis and respiration are reverse processes.

similar_questions.stem: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
similar_questions.answer: Carbon dioxide + water → (light, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen
explanation_steps: Light energy is trapped by chlorophyll.

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem:
Match the phrases in column A with the appropriate terms in column B. (3 points)
Column A: 12.1 Long sightedness; 12.2 Neurons; 12.3 Radicle; 12.4 Plumule; 12.5 Microscopic gap; 12.6 Short sightedness
Column B: A. Synapse; B. Root; C. Shoot; D. Myopia; E. Dendrites; F. Hypermetropia
explanation_steps: Long sightedness = hypermetropia (F); short sightedness = myopia (D) (G10 p.153).
Neurons have dendrites (E) that receive impulses; the microscopic gap between neurons is the synapse (A) (G10 p.164–166).
In germination the radicle develops into the root (B) and the plumule into the shoot (C) (G11 p.106).
marking_points: ½ point for each correct match
tips: Hyper-metropia: can see far (long sight); myopia: can see near (short sight).

similar_questions.stem: Which lens corrects (a) myopia and (b) hypermetropia?
explanation_steps: Myopic eyes focus in front of the retina; long-sighted eyes focus behind it.

questions.stem: Draw a complete flower and label it using the parts given: petal, anther, stigma, filament, style, ovary. (3 points)
questions.answer: A labelled longitudinal section of a complete flower: receptacle at the base with sepals; petals around the reproductive organs; stamens, each a filament (stalk) topped by an anther; a central pistil with the ovary at the base (containing ovules), the style above it and the stigma at the top.
explanation_steps: A complete flower has all four whorls: sepals, petals, stamens and pistil (carpel) (G11 p.129).
Stamen (male): filament supports the anther, a sac containing pollen grains.
Pistil (female): ovary (with ovules) at the base, style (stalk), stigma (sticky top that catches pollen).

Drawing guide: draw the receptacle, the ovary as a swelling in the centre, a style rising from it with a knob-shaped stigma; on each side draw thin filaments ending in anthers; draw petals outside the stamens and small sepals below them; label each part with a straight ruled line.
marking_points: Drawing of a recognisable complete flower (½ point)
Correct labelling of the six parts – petal, anther, stigma, filament, style, ovary (about ½ point each; teacher may scale so the total is 3)
Labels misplaced (e.g. anther on the stigma) earn no mark for that part
tips: Labels must touch the correct structure; drawings should be in pencil and without shading.

similar_questions.stem: Name the male and female parts of a flower and state the function of the stigma.
similar_questions.answer: Male: stamen (anther + filament); female: pistil/carpel (stigma, style, ovary). The stigma receives (catches) pollen grains.
explanation_steps: The sticky stigma traps pollen during pollination.

textbook_ref.section: 6.3 Sexual reproduction in plants – structure of a flower
